summary: Peta-nih is a decision-support dashboard that turns NASA Earth observations into plain-language crop-rotation advice for smallholder farmers. The user draws a field on a map, and PetaniH reads NASA POWER climate, SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rainfall, VIIRS and MODIS vegetation and land temperature, GEDI canopy and biomass, GRACE groundwater, SRTM terrain, and ISRIC SoilGrids soil data. It fuses them into a monthly grid and compares the farmer's current rotation with three alternatives (soil health, water saving, resilience). Each option gets eight scores computed with published methods (RUSLE erosion, FAO-56 crop water use, legume nitrogen fixation, residue carbon, ETCCDI climate extremes, Vegetation Condition Index), plus evidence, risks, and data gaps. Sliders for rainfall, temperature, and farmer priorities show how the ranking changes, and an optional AI assistant operates the dashboard and explains results briefly. Peta-nih supports, and does not replace, farmer judgment and local expertise.
details: Peta-nih helps smallholder farmers decide what to plant next using NASA satellite data. In Indonesia, and in many other tropical regions, farmers often grow rice season after season on the same land. This wears out the soil, lets pests build up, and makes the farm more exposed to dry spells and floods. Better crop rotation can help, but choosing a rotation means reading many kinds of information at once: weather, soil moisture, plant health, terrain, and soil quality. NASA collects most of this data, but it is spread across many services in formats that a farmer or an extension officer cannot easily use. We built Peta-nih to close that gap.Here is how it works. You draw your field on a map, or type its coordinates, and press one button. Peta-nih then runs a 12-step analysis for that exact location. It reads NASA POWER for temperature and rain, SMAP for soil moisture, GPM IMERG for rainfall rate, VIIRS and MODIS for vegetation greenness and land-surface temperature, GEDI for canopy height and biomass, GRACE for groundwater, SRTM for terrain and slope, and ISRIC SoilGrids for soil texture and carbon. The data is combined into a month-by-month picture of the field, with plain indicators for bare periods, heat stress, frost, extreme rain, long dry spells, water stress, vegetation stress, and whether the soil is getting drier over time.Next, Peta-nih compares your current rotation with three alternatives, each built around a different goal: soil health, water saving, and resilience to climate and pests. Every option is scored from 0 to 100 on overall value, soil health, water use, erosion, nitrogen, pest break, and climate fit. More importantly, each option comes with an explanation. It tells you why the rotation was suggested, which satellite or soil data supports it, what the benefits and risks are, where the data is incomplete, and what a local expert should still check before acting. You can move sliders to simulate less or more rain, hotter or cooler weather, or to say what matters most to you, such as saving water or improving soil, and watch the ranking change immediately. A map shows NASA imagery layers over your field, and a time-lapse button plays a layer back over the past year so you can see when the land was green, dry, or bare.We care most about trust. The scores are not guesses made by AI. They come from published scientific methods: the RUSLE equation for soil erosion, with rainfall erosivity calibrated for Java; FAO-56 for crop water needs; estimates of nitrogen fixed by legumes; organic carbon returned by crop residues; internationally agreed definitions of climate extremes; and the Vegetation Condition Index for plant stress. Every result shows its data source, date, and limitations. When data is missing, Peta-nih srally, and lists it as a gap instead ofinventing a number. For example, some NASA values are read from map imagery and are class midpoints rather than rawmeasurements, and three products (MODIS NDVInd ECOSTRESS) were unavailable duringdevelopment because their data provider was down. We also did not score market prices, because we had no reliableprice data.On the technical side, the frontend is javascript and angular the backend is written in Rust. The systemis deployed on a Linux server.The intended impact is healthier soil, more efficient water use, and more resilient harvests for smallholder farmers. Peta-nih is meant to support farmers, agronomin having better-informed conversations about rotation, not to replace their judgment or local knowledge
